title: Trini Stew Chicken
subtitle: Trinidadian chicken browned in caramel with green seasoning and scotch bonnet
excerpt: Chicken pieces marinated in green seasoning, then browned in burnt sugar and simmered until the sauce is thick and deeply savoury. The caramel browning is not optional. It defines the dish.
sourceNotes: Stew chicken is a cornerstone of Trinidadian home cooking. The burnt sugar browning technique is used across the Caribbean but is particularly central to Trini cuisine.

recipe.freezeNotes: Cool completely and freeze in the sauce. Defrost overnight and reheat on the hob over a low heat.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Marinate the chicken overnight for the best flavour. The green seasoning penetrates deeply with longer marinating.

content.text: Trini stew chicken gets its colour and depth from burning sugar until dark amber, then adding the chicken directly into the caramel. Work fast at that stage and keep a lid nearby in case it spits.
Toss the chicken pieces with the green seasoning, browning sauce, salt and pepper. Cover and refrigerate for at least 1 hour, or overnight.
Heat the oil and sugar together in a large heavy saucepan over a medium-high heat. Do not stir. Wait until the sugar melts and turns a deep amber brown, almost but not quite black.
Add the marinated chicken pieces in a single layer. They will spit. Turn quickly to coat them in the caramel. Brown for 3 minutes each side.
Push the chicken to the sides and add the onion and garlic to the centre. Cook for 2 minutes.
Add the scotch bonnet (left whole), thyme sprigs and chopped tomatoes. Stir everything together.
Pour in the water. Cover and simmer on a low heat for 30 minutes.
Remove the lid and cook for 10 more minutes until the sauce reduces and clings to the chicken. Remove the scotch bonnet and thyme stalks before serving.

items.symptom: The caramel seized and hardened when the chicken was added.
items.cause: The chicken was wet from the marinade, causing a sudden temperature drop.
items.fix: Pat the chicken dry before adding to the caramel. The coating will be less dramatic but still colour correctly.

items.symptom: The dish is too hot to eat.
items.cause: The scotch bonnet split during cooking and released its heat into the sauce.
items.fix: Keep the scotch bonnet whole and handle it carefully. If it splits, remove it immediately and taste frequently.

items.cause: The lid was on for too long and the sauce did not reduce.
items.fix: Remove the lid and increase the heat to medium. Simmer uncovered until the sauce thickens and coats the chicken.
